I like Schedule I. The core gameplay loop is genuinely fun, and the first playthrough is a great experience. Building your operation, unlocking new products, and gradually expanding your business is extremely satisfying.

Unfortunately, the game’s post-launch development has been disappointing. Content updates take far too long to reach production, and when they finally arrive, they often feel shallow and disconnected from the rest of the game.

The mushroom update is a good example. It gives you another product to manufacture, but it does not meaningfully affect the game. It does not change how you operate, introduce interesting decisions, or interact with the existing systems in a meaningful way. You can ignore mushrooms entirely and lose virtually nothing from the experience.

The cartel update was a fantastic idea with poor execution. A rival criminal organization should create pressure, competition, danger, and meaningful rewards. Instead, the cartel mostly adds more chores and obstacles without giving the player much to gain. It feels less like a dynamic rival and more like an artificial way to slow progression and stretch out the existing content. There was so much potential here, which makes the final result especially disappointing.

I understand that this is largely the work of a solo developer, and that game development takes time. However, that explanation becomes less convincing after a game earns millions of dollars. Players bought the game in Early Access to support its continued development. At some point, it is reasonable to expect some of that success to be reinvested into additional development resources, faster production, and more substantial updates.

Early Access was originally presented as a way for players to fund promising games while developers continued building them. Increasingly, it feels like a way to earn most of a game’s revenue before delivering a finished product. Players are not simply buying what currently exists; they are buying into a promise that the game will continue growing. When development slows down and updates feel minimal, it creates the impression that the game has entered maintenance mode before it is anywhere close to finished.

I love Schedule I, and I want to see it reach its potential. That is exactly why its current development and management are so frustrating. The foundation is excellent, but the time, money, and momentum generated by the game’s success do not seem to be translating into the depth or pace of development that players were led to expect.

Initially, during it's launch, I was put off by the Rick & Morty art-style when browsing my queue and skipped on it, incorrectly assuming it was just another shovel-ware release. I'm the fool.

Friend of mine talked about it and how enjoyable it was, so I decided to give the demo a shot and I was sold SUPER fast by the game-play loop. The art-style also quickly became really endearing and I found myself liking it enough to buy even before I'd completed the demo.

[b]The game offers :[/b]

- Multiple drugs to work with and ways to lace them, creating / naming your own products.
- Differently laced products have different effects, some are funny, some are functional.
- Multiple properties to own for the sake of creating product or laundering money.
- Multiple ways to sink money into infrastructure / business, employees or vehicles and clothes.
- Satisfying loop of creating product as well as harvesting it and packaging it.
- Physics based systems aren't everywhere, but where they are, they are fun.
- Lots of customers with different preferences for product types.
- A reasonably sized map that doesn't waste your time.
- Cops that hate you and want to touch you, a lot.
- Skateboards.
- Melee weapons and guns to defend yourself from crazed addicts or law enforcement.
- Freedom
- Online Co-Op / 4 Players

Honestly, what makes it a great game is the freedom to play it in whatever way you find enjoyable. You can be efficient, not so efficient, you can goof around, attack pretty much anyone, get them addicted to your stuff, you can pick up boxes and barrels during curfew, stack them and use them to climb over fences to avoid police patrols, you can hire employees or run your business solo and take the full cut and keep your gameplay loop, you can live a mundane lift of collecting trash for cash, etc.

It's incredibly fun, super affordable and it deserves your time & money to be honest.

Cracking game, great job with this one, it'll only get much better with time. Just don't squander the lightning in a bottle you have here. Don't work yourself to death, but stay consistent on updates and the community will love you & the game.

I’ve been playing Schedule One for a while now, and overall I genuinely enjoy it. The core gameplay loop is solid and it’s easy to sink hours into without noticing. If you like grind-heavy progression systems, this game will absolutely hook you. Watching your operation grow from nothing into something profitable is satisfying.

That said, the grind can feel excessive at times. A lot of the gameplay relies on repetitive manual tasks, and while that works early on, it starts to drag in the mid-to-late game. There needs to be deeper automation systems, something that lets you scale operations more efficiently once you’ve proven yourself.

Right now, it feels like you hit a ceiling. The game hints at building a serious empire, but you never quite reach that “kingpin” level. It would be great to expand progression so players can go full Tony Montana. Bigger networks, ability to export large quantities, larger territory control, higher risk/high reward systems, and more strategic management instead of constant micromanagement.

Schedule I takes the familiar structure of a business-management simulator and gives it an intentionally outrageous criminal twist. Developed and published by TVGS, it places players in Hyland Point with limited resources and the goal of building a small illicit operation into a much larger enterprise. The controversial premise is obviously part of its identity, but underneath the dark humor is a surprisingly detailed progression system. Production, sales, customer management, employees, properties, transportation, law enforcement, and expansion all contribute to a gameplay loop that continually gives the player something new to improve.

The early stages are deliberately hands-on. Players personally handle many of the jobs required to keep the business moving, from obtaining materials and preparing products to packaging goods and making deliveries. This creates an effective sense of starting from almost nothing. Money initially feels valuable because every purchase can influence efficiency. Better equipment, additional supplies, improved transportation, or access to another property can noticeably change how the operation functions. The result is a satisfying climb where success feels earned rather than immediately handed to the player.

Production provides much of the game's distinctive personality. Growing, processing, mixing, and packaging products involves direct interaction instead of reducing everything to background calculations. The mixing mechanics allow different ingredients and effects to be combined, creating plenty of experimentation and some intentionally ridiculous outcomes. These systems are straightforward enough to understand without making production completely passive. Repeating the same procedures can eventually become tedious, but that is also where the management progression becomes important.

Expansion gradually transforms the experience. Jobs that initially consume the player's time can increasingly be delegated to employees, allowing attention to shift toward larger decisions. Different workers can perform specialized duties associated with production, maintenance, sales, and other parts of the organization. Hiring staff is therefore more meaningful than simply increasing an efficiency statistic. A successful operation visibly becomes less dependent on the player performing every repetitive action personally. Building this transition from manual labor toward automation is one of the strongest aspects of the game.

Customer relationships and distribution provide another layer of progression. Producing large quantities means little without enough customers or an effective way to distribute the inventory. Dealers help extend the player's reach, while properties provide additional room for increasingly ambitious operations. Money management also becomes more complicated as profits increase, particularly because illegal earnings cannot always be treated like ordinary legitimate income. Businesses and money-laundering mechanics consequently become part of the broader strategy. These interconnected systems make expansion feel more substantial than simply watching a number increase.

Hyland Point itself helps prevent the game from feeling like a collection of management menus. Players physically travel through neighborhoods, meet people, visit businesses, transport goods, purchase equipment, and perform deliveries. Vehicles make larger journeys more manageable while reinforcing the sense that the criminal enterprise exists within an actual city. The stylized presentation is not technically extravagant, but its unusual characters and environments complement the deliberately absurd atmosphere. It feels more like a dark comedy sandbox than an attempt at realistic organized-crime simulation.

Law enforcement introduces risk into otherwise predictable routines. Suspicious behavior and criminal activity can lead to police attention, searches, arrests, roadblocks, curfews, and escalating wanted situations. Players therefore have reasons to consider how and when they move valuable inventory around the city. Combat is also available when circumstances become violent, although the shooting and fighting mechanics are not the primary attraction. The game is considerably stronger when its action systems support the business simulation rather than when they are treated as the main event.

Cooperative multiplayer fits the concept particularly well. Friends can divide responsibilities across production, deliveries, transportation, sales, and other tasks, turning the growing operation into a collaborative project. The game's unpredictable situations and exaggerated humor become even more entertaining when several players are involved. At the same time, solo play remains rewarding because managing everything personally makes the gradual transition toward employees and automation particularly noticeable.

Schedule I's biggest strength is how successfully its systems reinforce one another. Selling products produces money, money funds better infrastructure, improved infrastructure enables greater production, greater production creates demand for better distribution, and expansion eventually requires additional workers and properties. Each solution tends to create another objective. That interconnected progression gives the game its addictive quality. Even mundane activities feel worthwhile because they usually contribute toward a larger improvement.

As an Early Access title, it still has rough areas. Some activities become repetitive, portions of the simulation could benefit from additional depth, and occasional technical or interface imperfections remind players that development is continuing. Nevertheless, the underlying structure is already substantial. The combination of manual production, automation, exploration, business growth, police pressure, and cooperative play provides considerably more depth than the deliberately ridiculous premise might suggest.

On Steam Deck, Schedule I is classified as Playable rather than fully Verified. It can be played on the handheld and is generally practical for portable sessions, but the experience comes with qualifications. Some interactions may require touchscreen use, the virtual keyboard, or adjustments to the control configuration. Certain interface elements can display prompts that are not specifically designed for Steam Deck, and some text may be relatively small on the handheld display. Controller improvements have made the experience more comfortable, but players expecting completely seamless Deck integration should keep the Playable classification in mind.

Overall, Schedule I is an entertaining example of a provocative concept being supported by genuinely effective simulation mechanics. The pleasure comes less from its controversial subject matter than from watching a tiny operation evolve into an increasingly automated organization. Its strong progression, interconnected management systems, dark comedy, open-world structure, and enjoyable cooperative play provide plenty of reasons to continue expanding. Further Early Access development could make its weaker systems deeper and more polished, but the foundation is already remarkably engaging.

I bought this just a little over a week ago, and I've sunk over 100 hours into it. But I did what I set out to do and am now sitting happily in a kingdom that I built from the ground up all by myself. 

What a feverishly tedious journey it has been.

And so to conclude - I highly recommend this game. It's been an experience I'm sure I'll reflect upon, and will ultimately partake in again, but for now...I must rest.

Schedule I has a really fun concept, and the first few hours are genuinely enjoyable. Building your empire from scratch, managing production, and expanding your operation feels satisfying at the beginning. The progression system keeps you interested, and it’s easy to see why the game has become so popular on Steam.

However, after spending more time with it, the gameplay starts to feel repetitive. A lot of the tasks become part of the same grind loop, and the excitement slowly wears off. While the management mechanics are solid, the game currently lacks enough variety to keep things fresh for long sessions.

Since it’s still in Early Access, some parts also feel unpolished, with rough mechanics and occasional bugs. It definitely has strong potential, but right now it feels more like a great idea that still needs more content and refinement.

Overall, it’s a good game with a unique concept, but it can become repetitive after a while.

Schedule I totally caught me off guard. I thought I was just hopping into a basic sim, but nope—I ended up running a full-blown criminal empire and loving every second of it. It’s like Breaking Bad meets a tycoon game, and somehow it works way too well.

You start off small, juggling shady deliveries and managing your sketchy supplies, and suddenly you’re knee-deep in logistics, laundering cash like a pro, and trying not to collapse your entire operation. It’s stressful, chaotic, and absolutely addictive.

What makes it fun is how much you’re constantly solving problems—routes, timing, upgrades, cleaning dirty money—it all snowballs in the best way. I was legit proud when I pulled off a perfect run without blowing my cover.

Sure, the theme isn’t for everyone, but it’s played smartly, and the game doesn't take itself too seriously either. If you’re into management sims and want something a little darker but still super satisfying, Schedule I is a wild ride worth taking. Just don’t blame me when you're up at 2AM tweaking your delivery chain.

I wasn’t expecting much when I first booted up Schedule 1, but damn, this game goes way harder than I thought. It’s like Breaking Bad mixed with tycoon sim vibes and some co-op chaos, and somehow it just works. Bro, I legit lost track of time grinding this thing.

You start off broke, just tryna move a little product to get by, and next thing you know you’re running a full-on empire with grow rooms, dealers, labs, the whole nine. And it’s not some lazy clicker either, you actually gotta do the work. Trimming, mixing, bagging, running from the cops, doing shady deals - it’s messy, it’s dumb, and it’s hilarious.
The vibe is insane too. Goofy cartoon graphics mixed with dark humor, and somehow it nails it. You’re doing illegal stuff, but it’s all so over the top that you can’t help but laugh. Especially in co-op, man, when you’re playing with friends it just turns into pure madness. 

And yo, this was made by one dude. Like for real, one guy built all this, and it’s more fun and stable than half the AAA stuff I’ve played lately. No dumb bugs, no updates that break everything, it just runs and it’s actually fire.

Honestly, it’s one of those games you try for like 30 minutes and suddenly it’s 3am and you’re still going. If you’re into sims or just want something wild and different, this one’s 100 percent worth it. Might be the most fun I’ve had gaming this year, no lie.

Schedule I, really tickled my fancy. It just looked like it would be a bunch of fun, just lie back and chill out.
And I was 100% correct! It is an absolute bundle of fun. Highly recommended.

[B]POSITIVES:[/b]
[list]
[*]40+ hours of gameplay easily (I'm 20hrs in, and I haven't started producing a second drug type yet. I can see me playing around 60hrs, then taking a break for a few months until they have been a few more content updates)
[*]Super addictive gameplay (The irony)
[*]Fantastic mechanics, very well thought out and balanced. Huge number of possible recipes, different ways of running things - do it yourself to maximize profit or hire a team of workers and dealers do everything for you, balance of the two.
[*]Very funny moments, characters, and little Easter eggs (You can put Horse j!zz on your weed, who doesn't love that lol)
[*]Modding: there are already a few hundred mods available, and it's drag & drop, super easy.
[*] It runs well, no crashes or game-breaking bugs so far. Although a bit heavier on performance than I expected.
[*]Being in early access means there are frequent updates. Since I first saw this game a few months ago, there has already been so much more added. 
[/list]


[B]NEGATIVES:[/b]
[list]
[*]It is very easy. The police are more of a slight inconvenience. 
[*]Optimization issues. For a cartoon-style game, it's using 12GB of VRAM and 70-99% GPU usage on an RTX 3090, and I have the framerate capped at 120. It's using the same resources as GTA V!
[*]Definitely some pop-in issues. Even when you're just sprinting, there is some occasional nasty pop-in, much worse when you're traveling faster on a skateboard or vehicle
[*]Bug/Exploitable mechanic: [spoiler]You can do drug deals right in front of police officers just as long as you face away from them. If you turn away from them, they stop rendering (Occlusion Culling). So because they disappear, the script for them detecting you disappears, meaning you can walk in front of them at night or do a drug deal in front of their nose just as long as you face away from them.[/spoiler]
[/list]

[B]SUGGESTIONS:[/b]
Things I would like to see are all based around the game being very easy IMO, I don't want it to be Dark Souls, but the fact my 8-year-old niece is playing this with no issues and still hasn't been arrested tells me it's too easy. So I would like to see a difficulty option, like a "Hardcore mode" that adds:
[list]
[*]Simple things like increasing the prices of vehicles and properties so it takes longer to achieve them and makes them feel more of a long-term goal. I already had enough money for all of the properties within the first couple of days of playing.
[*]Customers being more picky or harder to negotiate with. At the moment you can upsell everyone massively.
[*]A hardcore mode should make the police more abundant, more foot/car patrols, pursue you for longer, call in backup, and spot you faster. (There are a couple of mods that do this already but they are a bit buggy)
[*]Variable yields from crops and cooks; instead of a guaranteed quantity, it varies with a higher percentage chance of lower yields and lower percentage chance of getting higher yields.
[*]This might already be in the game, and I just haven't encountered it yet (No spoilers please) but the occasional mugger or rival trying to hold you up to steal cash/drugs. Or even trying to raid your property to steal a bunch of resources.
[*]And of course, obvious ones like just expanding the map, adding new drug types, new components to mix, and new properties.
[*]I would love to see being able to create your own drug. A completely new and custom drug type is created by cooking lots of different chemicals and using different methods, so you end up with an inhaler that is like a cross between crack and ecstasy with a bit of bath salts mixed in.

I can see this game going gangbusters and having 10 times as much content in a year or two, I certainly hope so as there is so much potential to expand this even more. I can't wait to see what future updates bring.
Again, massive props and kudos to the creator.
